Introduction to Database Programming and SQL

Master the foundations of how modern applications store and manage data.

Welcome to the course. Today we bridge the gap between application code and persistent data storage.

Agenda

  • Client-Server Architecture
  • Software Layers and APIs
  • Relational Database Structure
  • Table Relationships
  • SQL Fundamentals: CRUD
  • Filtering and Sorting
  • Joining Tables
  • Data Integrity Best Practices
We will cover everything from hardware architecture to writing safe SQL queries.

Client-Server Architecture

  • Clients: Workstations or mobile devices
  • Network: LAN, WAN, or Internet
  • Server: Powerful machine hosting database
  • Supports multi-user distributed systems
Real-world business applications are rarely standalone; they rely on this three-component hardware stack.

Software Layers and APIs

  • Application: C# WinForms or Maui
  • Data Access API: ADO.NET/Entity Framework
  • DBMS: SQL Server processes queries
  • Database: Physical storage of data
The application doesn't touch the data directly; it uses an API to communicate with the Database Management System.

Relational Database Structure

  • Organized into logical tables
  • Tables consist of rows (records)
  • Columns represent specific attributes
  • Structured similarly to spreadsheets
Think of a database as a collection of related tables where each row is a unique entry.

Primary Keys

  • Uniquely identifies every row
  • Often an auto-generated integer
  • Safest filter for data modification
  • Avoid using names or emails
The Primary Key is the anchor of a table, ensuring no two records are confused.

Table Relationships

  • One-to-Many: Most common relationship
  • One-to-One: Employee to detail record
  • Many-to-Many: Requires junction table
  • Foreign Keys: Link related tables
Relationships allow us to connect data, like linking one customer to many different orders.

SQL Fundamentals: CRUD

  • Create: INSERT statement
  • Read: SELECT statement
  • Update: UPDATE statement
  • Delete: DELETE statement
CRUD represents the four basic operations you can perform on any data entity.

Basic Select Statement

SELECT * FROM Customers;
The asterisk is a wildcard that retrieves every column from the specified table.

Filtering and Sorting

  • WHERE clause filters specific rows
  • ORDER BY sorts the results
  • ASC for ascending order
  • DESC for descending order
Filtering and sorting allow you to narrow down thousands of records to exactly what you need.

Advanced Selection

SELECT ProductName, Price, Stock 
FROM Products 
WHERE Stock > 0 
ORDER BY Price DESC;
This example shows how to select specific columns, filter by a condition, and sort by price.

Joining Tables

  • Inner Joins combine related data
  • Matches columns between tables
  • Uses table aliases for readability
  • Links Primary and Foreign keys
Joins are essential for pulling data from multiple tables into a single result set.

Inner Join Example

SELECT C.CustomerName, O.OrderDate, O.OrderTotal 
FROM Customers AS C 
INNER JOIN Orders AS O ON C.CustomerID = O.CustomerID 
WHERE O.OrderTotal >= 100 
ORDER BY C.CustomerName ASC;
Notice the use of 'AS' to create aliases, making the query much easier to write and read.

Inserting Data

INSERT INTO Products (ProductName, Price, Stock) 
VALUES ('Wireless Keyboard', 49.99, 150);
When inserting, ensure the order of values matches the order of the columns specified.

Updating Records

UPDATE Customers 
SET Email = 'newemail@example.com', CityID = 12 
WHERE CustomerID = 1;
Always use the Primary Key in the WHERE clause to ensure you only update the intended record.

Deleting Records

DELETE FROM Products WHERE ProductID = 7;
Deletion is permanent; always double-check your filter criteria before executing.

Data Integrity Hazards

  • Missing WHERE: Updates every row
  • Missing WHERE: Deletes all data
  • Bad PK: Names can change
  • Always target specific IDs
A single missing WHERE clause can destroy an entire database table's integrity.

Best Practices

  • Use Primary Keys for filters
  • Understand low-level SQL syntax
  • Use aliases for complex joins
  • Verify logic before running Delete
Even if you use modern tools like ORMs, knowing the underlying SQL is vital for debugging.

Key Takeaways

  • SQL is a universal database language
  • One-to-many is the standard relationship
  • Always use WHERE with Update/Delete
  • Primary Keys ensure precise targeting
  • Tables use rows and columns
Remember these core principles to build safe and efficient database-driven applications.
